title: George Herbert
hookLine: a country parson poet: Love bade me welcome, yet my soul drew back
last: THE LANGUAGE OF HEAVEN, IN ENGLISH.

cards: A guest stands at an open door. The host says come in, you're welcome. And the guest hangs back on the step.
Muddy shoes. Empty hands. Not sure about a place at this table.
That stubborn hanging back is the whole subject of a short poem by an English country parson. It begins: "Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back".
The parson, the story goes, was a gifted man who could have had a career at court, and chose a small parish instead, writing poems that, tradition says, he wasn't even sure anyone should read.

teach.h: THE TEMPLE, PUBLISHED AFTER HIS DEATH.
teach.b: George Herbert was a priest in the Church of England. His poems were gathered in a book called The Temple, published after his death.
The story goes that he sent the manuscript to a friend, asking him to publish it if it might help some troubled soul, and to burn it if not. The friend published it.
The last poem in one part of the book is called Love, and it's a conversation at a door. Love invites the speaker in.
The speaker draws back, guilty of dust and sin. Love, quick-eyed, comes closer, asking gently if anything is lacking. A guest worthy to be here, the speaker answers.
Love says: you will be. I'm unkind and ungrateful, the speaker objects, I can't even look at you.

teach.h: WHO MADE THE EYES BUT I?
teach.b: Love takes his hand and smiles: who made the eyes but I? One last way out: if he can't be a guest, he'll work, and serve the meal. And Love says no: sit down, and taste my meat.
The poem ends with six plain words: "So I did sit and eat."

teach.h: SO I DID SIT AND EAT.
teach.b: No speech, no grand conversion. Just a person who stops arguing and accepts the seat. Some readers hear the Lord's Supper in it, Holy Communion.
Others hear the banquet of heaven, or simply the shape of grace. Either way, it can be harder to be welcomed than to be useful, and Herbert lets Love win the argument by being kind.

how: Herbert's poems are read in Anglican and other churches, and several have become hymns; the Church of England remembers him each year with a commemoration in its calendar.

games.q: you're the soul at Love's door. you've been welcomed, but you feel unworthy to be a guest. what do you do?
o: offer to serve the meal instead.
demand to know why you were invited.
games.why: the speaker tries to serve instead. but Love says no, sit down and taste my meat, and the poem ends: so I did sit and eat.

practice: If you can, find Herbert's Love, the third poem of that name, and read it slowly; if not, hold its first line and its last: love bade me welcome; so I did sit and eat.

Then sit, and notice where you hang back from being welcomed: by a person, by rest, by God if you believe in God. If you pray, simply accept the seat; if you don't, practice sitting without earning it.

wordCard.voice: George Herbert. An English country parson whose poem Love tells of a soul that draws back from welcome, argues, tries to serve instead, and finally sits down and eats.
